title: Social Media & the Attention Economy
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
A person can open an app intending to spend two minutes and stay for an hour. The interface matters because it changes when the person has to choose to stop.

Why does a small online task so often turn into a much longer session?
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: What stopping cue means
nodes.body:
A signal that an activity has reached a natural point where we can decide whether to continue.

For example: Finishing an article gives the reader an obvious place to close the tab.

One important limit: An endless feed often removes this pause.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: Finishing an article gives the reader an obvious place to close the tab. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports stopping cue. A signal that an activity has reached a natural point where we can decide whether to continue. An endless feed often removes this pause.
nodes.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: What habit cue means
nodes.body:

One important limit: A cue helps explain when behaviour starts; it does not determine every later choice.

nodes.title: What designed friction means
nodes.body:

For example: A feed starts another clip automatically, making stopping require a deliberate interruption.

One important limit: Friction can be adjusted to support autonomy; the same design does not affect everybody equally.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Riley has been trying to stop scrolling before bed. Ash notices Riley is still holding the phone an hour after opening an app.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.
nodes.scenario: Riley has been trying to stop scrolling before bed. Ash notices Riley is still holding the phone an hour after opening an app.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I meant to check one message. I've been scrolling for an hour.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What happened after you read it?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Another video loaded. I thought I'd stop after that one.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did you know what you were looking for next?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
checks.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

items.label: “I meant to check one message. I've been scrolling for an hour.”
An endless feed removes natural stopping cues while unpredictable interesting content makes the next item seem worth checking. The environment increases the work required to stop.
“What happened after you read it?”

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
An endless feed removes natural stopping cues while unpredictable interesting content makes the next item seem worth checking. The environment increases the work required to stop.

Another possibility: Riley may also be using the app to avoid a stressful evening or to connect socially; interface design is not the only influence.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare use when the next item requires a deliberate choice with use when content loads automatically. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare use when the next item requires a deliberate choice with use when content loads automatically.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Riley uses the same phone for reading long articles but stops easily when an article ends. The late-night problem is concentrated in the endless short-video feed.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The contrast strengthens the stopping-cue explanation, while leaving room for differences in interest and the social meaning of each platform.
nodes.counterexample: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Where did forty minutes go?
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of infinite scroll and delayed stopping cues.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Alter (2017), Irresistible; research on persuasive design and self-control.
nodes.scenario: Ada intended to watch one short cooking clip before going to sleep.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I opened the feed for one recipe and lost forty minutes.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Where did the app give you a natural chance to stop?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It didn't. The next clip started before I decided anything.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No. I kept thinking the next one might be better.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So continuing was easier than making a new choice each time.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Ada may be postponing bedtime because she does not want the day to end.
Ada may be enjoying the feed and choosing freely to watch longer than expected.
Automatic continuation and uncertain reward may be keeping Ada engaged beyond her initial intention.
The absence of an ending may matter more than unusually strong enjoyment of any individual video.
options.feedback: The repeated 'one more' decision is consistent with missing stopping cues.

options.label: Riley may be seeking social information about friends, making it harder to disengage from the app.
options.feedback: Social checking could explain persistence, but the described feed is dominated by short videos rather than messages.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Automatic continuation and uncertain reward may be keeping Ada engaged beyond her initial intention. Ada may be postponing bedtime because she does not want the day to end. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Frequent viewing is not automatically compulsive or harmful. The relevant question is whether the behaviour repeatedly conflicts with the person's goals.

checks.prompt: You are Ada. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Wait until the videos become boring enough that you naturally close the app.
options.reply: So continuing was easier than making a new choice each time.
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: Did you still want another clip?
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: Disable autoplay and decide the stopping point before opening the feed.
options.reply: That small delay changed the opportunity to act on the urge.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: The absence of an ending may matter more than unusually strong enjoyment of any individual video.
options.feedback: The repeated 'one more' decision is consistent with missing stopping cues.

checks.explanation: The first response addresses what can change. Asking about motives may help eventually; it need not be resolved before the concrete issue can be addressed.

nodes.title: What might change next?

nodes.conceptId: social-media-module-01:Variable reinforcement, friction and choice architecture

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?

nodes.title: A new situation

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
An endless feed removes natural stopping cues while unpredictable interesting content makes the next item seem worth checking. The environment increases the work required to stop.

Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

glossary.definition: A signal that an activity has reached a natural point where we can decide whether to continue.
glossary.example: Finishing an article gives the reader an obvious place to close the tab.
glossary.limit: An endless feed often removes this pause.

glossary.definition: A potentially enjoyable result whose timing or quality is uncertain.
glossary.example: Someone keeps scrolling because the next short video might be funnier.
glossary.limit: Not every repeated action reflects addiction; interest and habit also matter.

glossary.definition: A situation that begins prompting an action through repetition.
glossary.example: Picking up a phone automatically when sitting down before bed.
glossary.limit: A cue helps explain when behaviour starts; it does not determine every later choice.

glossary.definition: The amount of effort an interface makes us spend to begin or stop an action.
glossary.example: A feed starts another clip automatically, making stopping require a deliberate interruption.
glossary.limit: Friction can be adjusted to support autonomy; the same design does not affect everybody equally.
